{{Short description|Inequality applying to random variables}}
In [[information theory]], '''Fano's inequality''' (also known as the '''Fano converse''' and the '''Fano lemma''') relates the average information lost in a noisy channel to the probability of the categorization error.  It was derived by [[Robert Fano]] in the early 1950s while teaching a [[Ph.D.]] seminar in information theory at [[MIT]], and later recorded in his 1961 textbook.

It is used to find a lower bound on the error probability of any decoder as well as the lower bounds for [[minimax risk]]s in [[density estimation]].

Let the discrete [[random variables]] <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> represent input and output messages with a [[joint probability]] <math>P(x,y)</math>. Let <math>e</math> represent an occurrence of error; i.e., that <math>X\neq \tilde{X}</math>, with <math>\tilde{X}=f(Y)</math> being an approximate version of <math>X</math>. Fano's inequality is
:<math>H(X\mid Y)\leq H_b(e)+P(e)\log(|\mathcal{X}|-1),</math>

where <math>\mathcal{X}</math> denotes the support of <math>X</math>, <math>|\mathcal{X}|</math> denotes the [[cardinality]] of (number of elements in) <math>\mathcal{X}</math>,
:<math>H(X\mid Y)=-\sum_{i,j} P(x_i, y_j)\log P(x_i\mid y_j)</math>

is the [[conditional entropy]],
:<math>P(e)=P(X\neq\tilde{X})</math>

is the probability of the communication error, and
:<math>H_b(e)=-P(e)\log P(e)-(1-P(e))\log(1-P(e))</math>

is the corresponding [[Binary entropy function|binary entropy]].

==Proof==

Define an indicator random variable <math>E</math>, that indicates the event that our estimate <math>\tilde{X}=f(Y)</math> is in error,

:<math> E :=
\begin{cases}
1 ~&\text{ if }~ \tilde{X} \neq X~, \\
0 ~&\text{ if }~ \tilde{X} = X~.
\end{cases}
</math>

Consider <math>H(E,X|\tilde{X})</math>. We can use the [[Conditional entropy#Chain rule|chain rule for entropies]] to expand this in two different ways

:<math>
\begin{align}
H(E,X\mid\tilde{X}) &= H(X\mid\tilde{X}) + \underbrace{H(E\mid X,\tilde{X})}_{=0} \\
&= H(E\mid\tilde{X}) + H(X\mid E,\tilde{X})
\end{align}
</math>

Equating the two
:<math>
H(X\mid\tilde{X}) = H(E\mid\tilde{X}) + H(X\mid E,\tilde{X})
</math>

Expanding the right most term, <math>H(X\mid E,\tilde{X})</math>
:<math>
\begin{align}
H(X\mid E,\tilde{X}) &= \underbrace{H(X\mid E=0,\tilde{X})}_{=0}\cdot P(E=0) + H(X\mid E=1,\tilde{X})\cdot\underbrace{P(E=1)}_{=P(e)} \\
                 &= H(X\mid E=1,\tilde{X})\cdot P(e)
\end{align}
</math>
Since <math>E=0</math> means <math>X=\tilde{X}</math>; being given the value of <math>\tilde{X}</math> allows us to know the value of <math>X</math> with certainty. This makes the term <math>H(X\mid E=0,\tilde{X}) = 0</math>.
On the other hand, <math>E=1</math> means that <math>\tilde{X}\neq X</math>, hence given the value of <math>\tilde{X}</math>, we can narrow down <math>X</math> to one of <math>|\mathcal{X}|-1</math> different values, allowing us to upper bound the conditional entropy <math>H(X\mid E=1,\tilde{X}) \leq \log(|\mathcal{X}|-1)</math>. Hence

:<math> H(X\mid E,\tilde{X}) \leq \log(|\mathcal{X}|-1)\cdot P(e). </math>

The other term, <math>H(E\mid\tilde{X}) \leq H(E)</math>, because conditioning reduces entropy. Because of the way <math>E</math> is defined, <math>H(E) = H_b(e)</math>, meaning that <math>H(E\mid\tilde{X}) \leq H_b(e)</math>. Putting it all together,

:<math> H(X\mid\tilde{X}) \leq H_b(e) + P(e)\log(|\mathcal{X}|-1) </math>

Because <math> X \rightarrow Y \rightarrow \tilde{X} </math> is a [[Markov chain]], we have <math>I(X;\tilde{X}) \leq I(X;Y)</math> by the [[data processing inequality]], and hence <math> H(X\mid\tilde{X}) \geq H(X\mid Y) </math>, giving us

:<math> H(X\mid Y) \leq H_b(e) + P(e)\log(|\mathcal{X}|-1) </math>

==Intuition==
'''Fano's inequality''' can be interpreted as a way of dividing the uncertainty of a conditional distribution into two questions given an arbitrary predictor. The first question, corresponding to the term <math> H_b(e) </math>, relates to the uncertainty of the predictor. If the prediction is correct, there is no more uncertainty remaining. If the prediction is incorrect, the uncertainty of any [[Probability distribution|discrete distribution]] has an upper bound of the entropy of the uniform distribution over all choices besides the incorrect prediction. This has entropy <math> \log(|\mathcal{X}|-1) </math>. Looking at extreme cases, if the predictor is always correct the first and second terms of the inequality are 0, and the existence of a perfect predictor implies <math> X </math> is totally determined by <math> Y </math>, and so <math> H(X|Y) = 0 </math>. If the predictor is always wrong, then the first term is 0, and  <math> H(X\mid Y) </math> can only be upper bounded with a uniform distribution over the remaining choices.

==Alternative formulation==
Let <math>X</math> be a [[random variable]] with [[Probability density function|density]] equal to one of <math>r+1</math> possible densities <math>f_1,\ldots,f_{r+1}</math>. Furthermore, the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]] between any pair of densities cannot be too large,
:<math> D_{KL}(f_i\parallel f_j)\leq \beta</math> for all <math>i\not = j.</math>

Let <math>\psi(X)\in\{1,\ldots, r+1\}</math> be an estimate of the index. Then

:<math>\sup_i P_i(\psi(X)\not = i) \geq 1-\frac{\beta+\log 2}{\log r}</math>
where <math>P_i</math> is the [[probability]] induced by <math>f_i</math>.

==Generalization==
The following generalization is due to Ibragimov and Khasminskii (1979), Assouad and Birge (1983).

Let '''F''' be a class of densities with a subclass of ''r''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 densities ''ƒ''<sub>''θ''</sub> such that for any ''θ''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;''θ''<nowiki>′</nowiki>

:<math>\|f_{\theta}-f_{\theta'}\|_{L_1}\geq \alpha,</math>
:<math>D_{KL}(f_\theta\parallel f_{\theta'})\leq \beta.</math>

Then in the worst case the [[expected value]] of error of estimation is bounded from below,

:<math>\sup_{f\in \mathbf{F}} E \|f_n-f\|_{L_1}\geq \frac{\alpha}{2}\left(1-\frac{n\beta+\log 2}{\log r}\right)</math>

where ''ƒ''<sub>''n''</sub> is any [[density estimation|density estimator]] based on a [[sample (statistics)|sample]] of size ''n''.
